_readme: Starter content for the Coaching Lab. Everything here is an unreviewed DRAFT by "Mathlete draft" and stays off the live site until a coach reviews and publishes it in the CMS. Loaded into Supabase by supabase/coaching-seed.sql (node scripts/build-coaching.mjs regenerates that file after you change this one). Re-running the seed only adds ids that are not in the database yet.

people.name: Mathlete draft
people.bio: Placeholder starter content written to show the lesson structure. Every lesson credited here must be rewritten or reviewed by a qualified coach before it is published.

disciplines.name: MTB Foundations
disciplines.summary: The core movements every other skill is built from.

disciplines.name: Downhill
disciplines.summary: Descending fast and in control on steep, technical gravity trails.

disciplines.name: Jumping & Airtime
disciplines.summary: Leaving the ground on purpose, and coming back down smoothly.

disciplines.name: Dirt Jumping
disciplines.summary: Purpose-built dirt lines: timing, lip awareness and trick progression.

disciplines.name: Slopestyle & Freestyle
disciplines.summary: Aerial awareness and tricks. High-consequence content needs specialist coaching.

disciplines.name: Bike Control & Tricks
disciplines.summary: Moving the bike underneath you: wheel lifts, manuals, hops and pivots.

disciplines.name: Enduro & Trail Riding
disciplines.summary: Riding real trails well, up and down, for a long day.

disciplines.name: Bike Setup & Equipment
disciplines.summary: A bike that fits and is set up well makes every skill easier.

competencies.name: Stability & Balance
competencies.description: Keeping rider and bike stable over the tyres, moving or still, and recovering when balance shifts.

competencies.name: Controls
competencies.description: Precise use of brakes, pedals, grips and dropper: how much, when and how smoothly.

competencies.name: Terrain Awareness
competencies.description: Reading the trail ahead: surfaces, gradients, features and lines, early enough to act on them.

competencies.name: Direction Control
competencies.description: Choosing and holding a line through steering, leaning the bike and looking where you want to go.

competencies.name: Pressure Control
competencies.description: Managing how hard the tyres press into the ground: absorbing, pushing and unweighting the bike.

competencies.name: Timing & Coordination
competencies.description: Linking movements in the right order at the right moment, often in a fraction of a second.

drills.name: Slow Line Race
drills.objective: Build low-speed control by riding a line as slowly as possible.
steps: Mark a straight lane 10-15 m long.
Ride it as slowly as you can without putting a foot down.
Repeat, trying to take longer each time.
Make the lane narrower when it feels easy.
drills.environment: Flat, open area such as a car park, field or pump track apron
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
success: You complete the lane without a foot down
Your time gets longer over attempts

drills.name: Track Stand Progression
drills.objective: Learn to balance with the bike stopped.
steps: Face a slight uphill so gravity helps you hold position.
Turn the bars a little toward your front foot.
Rock gently against the pedal and brake to stay balanced.
Count how long you can hold it; aim for 5 seconds, then 10.
drills.environment: Flat, open area such as a car park, field or pump track apron
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
Practise near a wall or fence you can reach if you lose balance
success: Holds for 5 seconds
Recovers small wobbles without a foot down

drills.name: Ready Position Check
drills.objective: Find and feel a balanced ready position.
steps: Roll slowly on flat ground in the ready position.
Have a friend gently push and pull the bike; stay balanced.
Rise tall, then go low, then return to centre.
Repeat while rolling.
drills.environment: Flat, open area such as a car park, field or pump track apron
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
success: Bike can move under you without you losing balance
Hands stay light on the grips

drills.name: Bike-Body Separation
drills.objective: Move the bike independently of your body.
steps: Roll slowly in the ready position.
Lean the bike left and right underneath you while your body stays upright.
Push the bike forward and draw it back without your chest moving much.
Build to smooth, continuous movement.
drills.environment: Flat, open area such as a car park, field or pump track apron
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
success: Bike leans while your head stays level
Movements are smooth, not jerky

drills.name: Stop Box
drills.objective: Stop smoothly in a target zone using both brakes.
steps: Mark a 2 m box at the end of a straight 20 m lane.
Ride toward it at a steady speed.
Brake smoothly with both brakes to stop inside the box without skidding.
Increase speed gradually as you get consistent.
drills.environment: Flat, open area such as a car park, field or pump track apron
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
success: Stops in the box without skidding
Body stays balanced, heels down

drills.name: Brake Before the Turn
drills.objective: Separate braking from turning.
steps: Set a cone 10 m before a wide turn.
Finish all your braking before the cone.
Release the brakes and roll through the turn.
Move the cone closer to the turn as you improve.
drills.environment: Flat, open area such as a car park, field or pump track apron
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
success: Brakes released before turning
Smooth, steady speed through the turn

drills.name: Call the Cone
drills.objective: Practise looking ahead by reacting to signals early.
steps: Ride a loop with a friend standing ahead holding up a coloured card.
Call out the colour as soon as you see it.
Have them change the card at different distances.
Notice how early you can call it when your eyes are up.
drills.environment: Flat, open area such as a car park, field or pump track apron
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
success: You call colours early and consistently
Your riding stays smooth while looking up

drills.name: Walk the Line
drills.objective: Plan a line through a section before riding it.
steps: Pick a short section of easy trail with a few features.
Walk it and choose your entry, path and exit.
Ride it following your plan.
Walk it again and adjust.
drills.environment: Easy trail section with a few roots, rocks or turns
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
success: You can describe your line before riding
You ride the line you planned

drills.name: Cone Slalom
drills.objective: Develop steering and leaning control.
steps: Set 6-8 cones in a line about 3 m apart.
Weave through slowly, looking ahead to the next gap.
Narrow the spacing as it gets easier.
Try leaning the bike more and steering less.
drills.environment: Flat, open area such as a car park, field or pump track apron
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
success: Weaves through without hitting cones
Eyes are on the next gap, not the current cone

drills.name: Figure Eight
drills.objective: Practise turning both ways smoothly.
steps: Mark two cones about 6 m apart.
Ride a figure eight around them.
Shrink the eight over time.
Keep the bike leaning and your eyes leading.
drills.environment: Flat, open area such as a car park, field or pump track apron
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
success: Smooth turns both directions
No foot down

drills.name: Apex Cones
drills.objective: Learn a good corner line.
steps: Set an entry cone wide, an apex cone on the inside and an exit cone wide.
Ride the line through all three.
Finish braking before the entry cone.
Move the apex later as you improve.
drills.environment: Flat, open area such as a car park, field or pump track apron
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
success: Rides wide-tight-wide line
Brakes released before the entry cone

drills.name: Roller Absorb
drills.objective: Learn to absorb and extend over rollers.
steps: Roll over a series of small rollers without pedalling.
Let the bike rise into you on the way up.
Push it down the back side of each roller.
Try to keep your head at the same height.
drills.environment: Gentle rollers on a pump track or trail
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
success: Head stays level
Speed carried without pedalling

drills.name: No-Pedal Pump Laps
drills.objective: Build pumping rhythm.
steps: Start a lap on a pump track with a few pedal strokes.
Try to complete the lap without pedalling.
Count how many rollers you can pump before slowing too much.
Aim to add one roller each session.
drills.environment: Pump track
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
Ride in the same direction as other riders
Wait for a clear track before starting
success: Completes more rollers each attempt
Speed maintained without pedalling

drills.name: Lift and Land
drills.objective: Lift and set down the front wheel smoothly.
steps: Roll slowly on level pedals.
Sink down, then shift your hips back to lift the front wheel a few centimetres.
Set it down gently.
Repeat 10 times; then try over a chalk line.
drills.environment: Flat, open area such as a car park, field or pump track apron
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
success: Front wheel lifts without pulling on the bars
Lands smoothly

drills.name: Curb Roll-Up
drills.objective: Use a front-wheel lift on a real feature.
steps: Find a low curb or step (5-10 cm).
Approach slowly in the ready position.
Lift the front wheel onto the step.
Push the bike forward to roll the rear up.
drills.environment: Low curb or step 5-10 cm high
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
success: Front wheel clears the step
Rear rolls up smoothly

drills.name: Rear-Wheel Lift
drills.objective: Learn to lift the rear wheel on its own.
steps: Roll slowly in the ready position.
Shift your weight forward and push the bars forward.
Lift your feet with the pedals to bring the rear up.
Start tiny; aim for a few centimetres.
drills.environment: Flat, open area such as a car park, field or pump track apron
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
Keep speed low
Do not use clipless pedals for this drill until consistent
success: Rear wheel lifts without the front coming up
Controlled landing

drills.name: Hop the Line
drills.objective: Link front and rear lifts.
steps: Draw a chalk line or lay a pool noodle on the ground.
Roll toward it slowly.
Lift the front, then the rear, to clear it.
Only raise the obstacle once you clear it every time.
drills.environment: Flat, open area such as a car park, field or pump track apron
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
Use soft obstacles that move if hit
Never use rigid obstacles while learning
success: Both wheels clear the line
Front lands first or both together

drills.name: Tabletop Roll-Over
drills.objective: Learn the shape of a jump at low speed.
steps: Find a small tabletop.
Roll over it at low speed with both wheels on the ground.
Practise absorbing the face and extending down the landing.
Gradually add a little speed until the wheels just leave the ground.
drills.environment: Small tabletop jump with a flat deck
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
Inspect the jump before riding
Wait for the landing to be clear
Only go bigger once every run is consistent
success: Wheels leave the lip together
Landing on the deck or the top of the landing

drills.name: Small Drop-Off
drills.objective: Practise landings at low height.
steps: Find a 10-20 cm drop with a smooth landing.
Roll off slowly, keeping both wheels level.
Absorb the landing with arms and legs.
Repeat until every landing is smooth.
drills.environment: A curb or ledge 10-20 cm high with a smooth landing
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
Check the landing is clear and smooth
Keep speed low
success: Both wheels land together
Rider absorbs and rides away smoothly

drills.name: Find the Balance Point
drills.objective: Feel where the balance point is with brake control.
steps: On grass, roll slowly with a finger on the rear brake.
Lift the front and keep shifting back until it feels like it might loop.
Dab the rear brake to bring the front down.
Repeat, getting closer to the balance point each time.
drills.environment: Flat grass or a smooth car park
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
Always cover the rear brake
Practise on grass when learning to loop out
Use flat pedals so you can step off the back
success: Uses the rear brake to recover every time
Holds the front up a little longer each attempt

drills.name: Pressure Test Loop
drills.objective: Find your tyre pressure by testing.
steps: Ride a short loop with a few corners at your starting pressure.
Note how the tyres feel.
Change pressure slightly and ride again.
Keep notes of what felt best for each kind of trail.
drills.environment: A short familiar loop
safety: Wear a helmet and gloves
Check brakes work before you start
success: You have a written pressure for each trail type
Tyres grip without squirming or bottoming

mistakes.name: Eyes on the front wheel
mistakes.description: Looking down at the ground right in front of you.
mistakes.looks_like: Head tilted down, frequent wobbles, late reactions.
mistakes.cause: Nerves or concentrating too hard on the bike instead of the path.
mistakes.correction: Pick a point 5-10 m ahead and keep your eyes there. Your peripheral vision handles what is close.

mistakes.name: Death grip on the bars
mistakes.description: Holding the grips so tightly that the bike can't move under you.
mistakes.looks_like: White knuckles, locked elbows, the whole body moves with every bump.
mistakes.cause: Tension and trying to control the bike through your hands.
mistakes.correction: Hold the grips firmly enough to control them, no more. Let your weight go through your feet.

mistakes.name: Locked arms and legs
mistakes.description: Standing tall and stiff with straight elbows and knees.
mistakes.looks_like: Rider looks upright and rigid, bounced around by small bumps.
mistakes.cause: Nervousness, or not knowing that bent limbs are the goal.
mistakes.correction: Lower your chest and bend your elbows until they point slightly out. Let the bike move under you.

mistakes.name: Hanging off the back
mistakes.description: Pushing the hips far behind the saddle, especially on steeper ground.
mistakes.looks_like: Arms straight, front wheel light and hard to steer.
mistakes.cause: Fear of going over the bars on descents.
mistakes.correction: Stay centred over the pedals relative to gravity. Move back only as much as the slope needs, with your arms still bent.

mistakes.name: Rear brake only
mistakes.description: Using only the rear brake, often from fear of the front.
mistakes.looks_like: Long skid marks, slow stops, rear wheel sliding.
mistakes.cause: Worry that the front brake will throw you over the bars.
mistakes.correction: Practise smooth front braking on flat ground with your heels down. The front brake does most of the stopping when you're braced.

mistakes.name: Braking in the corner
mistakes.description: Grabbing the brakes while already turning.
mistakes.looks_like: Bike stands up and runs wide, or the front tyre slides.
mistakes.cause: Entering too fast and reacting late.
mistakes.correction: Do your braking before the turn, on the straight, so you can release and let the tyres grip through it.

mistakes.name: Target fixation
mistakes.description: Staring at the obstacle you want to avoid.
mistakes.looks_like: Rider rides straight into the rock or tree they were worried about.
mistakes.cause: Your bike tends to go where your eyes go.
mistakes.correction: Look at the gap or line you want to ride, not at the obstacle.

mistakes.name: Leaning with the bike
mistakes.description: Tilting your whole body with the bike like a motorbike racer.
mistakes.looks_like: Rider and bike lean as one; front tyre washes out on loose surfaces.
mistakes.cause: Copying road or motorbike riding, or not separating body and bike.
mistakes.correction: Keep your body more upright and press the bike down underneath you.

mistakes.name: Turning in too early
mistakes.description: Cutting to the inside at the start of the corner.
mistakes.looks_like: Bike runs wide on exit, rider brakes mid-corner or leaves the trail.
mistakes.cause: Eagerness to get round, eyes on the inside edge.
mistakes.correction: Stay wide longer and look for the exit before turning in. Aim for a late apex.

mistakes.name: Pushing on the upslope
mistakes.description: Pushing into the face of the roller instead of the back side.
mistakes.looks_like: Rider slows down on every roller despite working hard.
mistakes.cause: Timing is early, usually from looking at the roller underneath you.
mistakes.correction: Look one roller ahead and wait to push until the wheel crests the top.

mistakes.name: Pulling on the bars
mistakes.description: Yanking the bars up with your arms.
mistakes.looks_like: Bent arms, a short twitchy lift, rider tires quickly.
mistakes.cause: It feels like the obvious way to lift the front.
mistakes.correction: Push down first, then shift your hips back with straight arms. Let your weight do the lifting.

mistakes.name: Lifting both wheels at once
mistakes.description: Pulling up with hands and feet together (a "pull-up" hop).
mistakes.looks_like: Low hop, rear lands first, bike feels heavy.
mistakes.correction: Separate the two parts. Practise the front lift and rear lift on their own, then link them slowly.

mistakes.name: Braking on the jump face
mistakes.description: Dragging the brakes as you ride up the takeoff.
mistakes.looks_like: Bike pitches nose-down off the lip, rider comes up short.
mistakes.cause: Doubt about speed, so the brakes come on at the last moment.
mistakes.correction: Set your speed earlier on the approach and keep your fingers off the levers on the face. If in doubt, roll it.

mistakes.name: Nose-diving (bucking)
mistakes.description: The rear of the bike kicks up off the lip.
mistakes.looks_like: Bike pitches nose-down in the air; rider is thrown forward.
mistakes.cause: Riding the lip stiffly or pushing late, so the rear wheel is pushed up hard.
mistakes.correction: Let the bike come up through the lip with soft legs, staying centred.

mistakes.name: Guessing the speed
mistakes.description: Hitting a jump without knowing how fast to go.
mistakes.looks_like: Coming up short onto the deck edge, or overshooting the landing.
mistakes.correction: Start slow and add a little speed each run, so you always know what the last run felt like.

mistakes.name: Bent arms in the manual
mistakes.description: Holding the manual with bent elbows.
mistakes.looks_like: Front wheel bobs up and down, short manuals, arms tire fast.
mistakes.cause: Using your arms to hold the front up.
mistakes.correction: Straighten your arms and let your hips do the work. Your arms are only connecting you to the bars.

mistakes.name: Rolling a drop too slowly
mistakes.description: Creeping off a drop that's too big to roll.
mistakes.looks_like: Front wheel drops first, rider is pitched forward.
mistakes.correction: Match speed to the drop, release the brakes before the edge and add a small front lift.

mistakes.name: Tyres pumped too hard
mistakes.description: Running road-bike-like pressures on the trail.
mistakes.looks_like: Bike skips and bounces, tyres slide on roots and rocks.
mistakes.cause: Assuming higher pressure is faster or safer.
mistakes.correction: Lower pressure a little at a time and test. Most trail tyres need far less than the maximum on the sidewall.

skills.name: Balance and Stability
skills.summary: Stay steady over the bike at low speed and when standing still, so every other skill has a stable base.
skills.why_it_matters: Balance is the base layer of mountain biking. Riders who can stay calm and steady at walking pace handle tight switchbacks, technical climbs and slow, awkward moves without putting a foot down, and they have more attention left for the trail.

skills.name: Body Positioning
skills.summary: The ready position: balanced, relaxed and able to move with the bike over any terrain.
skills.environment: Flat open ground, then gentle trail
skills.why_it_matters: Almost every technical skill starts from a good ready position. It lets your legs and arms work as suspension, keeps your weight where the tyres need it, and gives you room to move forward, back, up and down as the trail changes.

skills.name: Braking Fundamentals
skills.summary: Slow down and stop with control, using both brakes and good body position.
skills.environment: Flat open area, then a gentle gravel or dirt slope
skills.why_it_matters: Good braking is what lets you ride faster safely. Riders who brake smoothly, mostly with the front brake and before a feature rather than in it, keep traction and stay in control on steep and technical trails.

skills.name: Terrain Awareness
skills.summary: Look ahead, read the trail and choose a line early enough to ride it well.
skills.environment: Easy trail with a mix of surfaces
skills.why_it_matters: Where you look decides where you go and how much time you have to react. Riders who look further ahead ride smoother, choose better lines and feel less rushed, because they see what's coming before they reach it.

skills.name: Direction Control
skills.summary: Steer and lean the bike to hold a chosen line, at low and moderate speed.
skills.environment: Flat open area with cones, then easy trail
skills.why_it_matters: Holding a line is what lets you ride narrow singletrack, avoid obstacles and set up for corners. Direction control combines steering with leaning the bike and looking through the turn.

skills.name: Cornering Fundamentals
skills.summary: Enter, turn and exit corners smoothly: braking, line, lean and vision working together.
skills.environment: Wide, smooth flat corners, then berms on easy trail
skills.why_it_matters: Trails are full of corners. Good cornering keeps you safe, saves energy and is one of the biggest sources of speed, because you can carry momentum through the turn instead of braking hard and pedalling back up to speed.

skills.name: Pressure Control
skills.summary: Push the bike into the ground and let it rise, to absorb bumps and add grip.
skills.environment: Gentle rollers or a pump track, or a grassy slope with small bumps
skills.why_it_matters: Pressure control is the hidden skill behind smooth riding. It lets you absorb rough ground, keep your tyres pressing into the trail for grip, and make the bike light when you need to lift it.

skills.name: Pumping
skills.summary: Generate speed without pedalling by pushing into the back of rollers and berms.
skills.environment: Pump track or rollers on a flow trail
skills.why_it_matters: Pumping turns the shape of the trail into speed. It also trains the timing and pressure control you need for jumping, and makes flow trails much more fun.

skills.name: Front-Wheel Lifts
skills.summary: Lift the front wheel briefly to clear small obstacles and prepare for manuals and hops.
skills.environment: Flat smooth area, then small curbs or roots
skills.why_it_matters: Lifting the front wheel lets you roll onto curbs and over roots without slamming into them. It's also the first step toward manuals, bunny hops and drops.

skills.name: Bunny Hop Foundations
skills.summary: Lift both wheels off the ground to clear obstacles, using a front lift then a rear lift.
skills.environment: Flat smooth area with a soft line or low foam obstacle
skills.learning_commitment: Usually several sessions to link the movements consistently
skills.why_it_matters: A bunny hop lets you clear logs, roots and gaps, and teaches the coordination behind jumping and many tricks.

skills.name: Jumping Fundamentals
skills.summary: Ride small tabletop jumps smoothly: speed, takeoff, a calm flight and a soft landing.
skills.environment: Small, well-built tabletop jumps at a bike park or pump track
skills.learning_commitment: Several sessions on small jumps before moving to bigger ones
skills.why_it_matters: Jumping smoothly is one of the most rewarding skills in mountain biking. It also matters for safety: a well-ridden takeoff keeps the bike level and predictable in the air.

skills.name: Landing Fundamentals
skills.summary: Land smoothly after drops and jumps by matching the bike to the slope and absorbing the impact.
skills.environment: Small rollers, then small drops with a downslope landing
skills.why_it_matters: Most jump and drop crashes happen on landing. Learning to match the bike to the landing and absorb it well makes every airborne skill safer.

skills.name: Manual Foundations
skills.summary: Ride on the rear wheel without pedalling, balancing with your hips and the rear brake.
skills.environment: Flat, smooth surface such as a car park or grass, away from traffic
skills.learning_commitment: Most riders need many short sessions over several weeks
skills.why_it_matters: Manuals help you roll over gaps, absorb rollers and keep momentum through rough sections. They also build balance and confidence moving your weight on the bike.

skills.name: Drops
skills.summary: Ride off small ledges and drops with the right speed and a level bike.
skills.environment: Small, well-built drops with a clean downslope landing
skills.why_it_matters: Drops appear on many trails, from small rock steps to built features. Riding them with the right speed and a level bike is the difference between a smooth roll and a front-wheel-first landing.

skills.name: Bike Setup Fundamentals
skills.summary: Set tyre pressure, suspension sag and controls so the bike fits you and every skill feels easier.
skills.environment: At home or the trailhead, with a pump and shock pump
skills.why_it_matters: A badly set-up bike makes good technique harder. Getting tyre pressure, suspension sag and lever position close to right gives you grip, comfort and control.

lessons.title: Balance and Stability Foundations
lessons.introduction: Balancing a bike is mostly about keeping your combined centre of mass over the small patch where the tyres touch the ground. At speed the bike helps you; at walking pace you have to do more of the work. This lesson builds that low-speed control.
objectives: Ride a straight line at walking pace without wobbling
Hold a track stand for a few seconds
Explain why moving the bars and hips keeps you upright

physics.summary: You stay upright by keeping your centre of mass above your base of support: the line between your two tyre contact patches.

blocks.heading: Your base of support is a thin line
blocks.body: Standing on two feet you have a wide base. On a bike, your base is just the line between two contact patches a few centimetres wide. When your centre of mass drifts to one side of that line, gravity creates a torque that tips you further. You correct it by steering the wheels back underneath you or by moving your body.

blocks.heading: Why slow is harder than fast
blocks.body: At speed, small steering inputs move the contact patches under you quickly, so corrections are easy. Spinning wheels add a little stability too, but less than most people think. At walking pace both effects shrink, so your body movements and small bar and brake inputs do more of the balancing.

technique.title: Neutral stance
technique.result: A relaxed, balanced position you can move from in any direction.
technique.movement: Stand on level pedals, knees and elbows soft, eyes up. Weight through your feet, not your hands.
technique.interaction: The bike can move under you without pulling you off balance.
cues: Look where you want to go, not at the front wheel

technique.title: Slow-speed line
technique.result: Ride slowly in a straight line without wobbling.
technique.movement: Keep a little pedal pressure against light rear brake drag. Make small bar movements and let the bike lean slightly under you.
technique.interaction: Pedal against brake gives you fine control of speed.
cues: Eyes on a point well ahead
errors: Looking down at the front wheel

technique.title: Track stand
technique.movement: Turn the bars slightly toward your front foot. Use small forward and back pedal movements against the brake to rock the bike and keep your weight centred.
technique.interaction: Rocking forward and back shifts the contact patch sideways because the wheel is turned.

equipment: A bike in good working order, sized to fit you
protective: Flat or clip-in shoes with good grip
conditions: Avoid wet or loose surfaces while learning
stop_conditions: You feel tired, frustrated or rushed
The surface becomes wet, muddy or loose
Anything on the bike feels loose or wrong

lessons.title: Body Positioning Foundations
lessons.introduction: The ready position (often called the attack position) is a relaxed, athletic stance on level pedals. It is not a fixed pose: it is a central place you move away from and back to as the trail demands.
objectives: Find a balanced ready position on level pedals
Move forward, back, up and down from it while rolling
Explain why your weight should go through your feet

physics.summary: Where your centre of mass sits relative to the wheels decides how much load each tyre carries, which affects grip, braking and how the bike reacts to bumps.

blocks.heading: Centred mass, balanced grip
blocks.body: With your hips roughly over the bottom bracket, weight is shared between the tyres. Move your hips back and the rear tyre carries more; move forward and the front does. On steep ground gravity shifts load toward the front wheel, so you move back a little to stay centred relative to gravity, not relative to the bike.

blocks.heading: Your limbs are suspension
blocks.body: Bent knees and elbows can extend and compress, soaking up bumps the bike's suspension can't. Locked joints pass every hit straight into your body and off-balance you.

technique.title: Level pedals
technique.result: A stable platform for your feet.
technique.movement: Pedals at 3 and 9 o'clock, weight through the balls of your feet, heels slightly dropped.
technique.interaction: Both feet share the load, so the bike stays level under you.

technique.title: Hinge and bend
technique.result: A low, athletic stance with room to move.
technique.movement: Bend at the hips so your chest comes forward, knees and elbows bent and pointing slightly out.
technique.interaction: Bent joints give you range to push and absorb.

technique.title: Move with the bike
technique.result: Stay centred as the terrain changes.
technique.movement: Let the bike move under you: push it into dips, let it come up over bumps, shift back a little on descents.
technique.interaction: Your centre of mass follows a smoother path than the bike.
cues: Centred over the pedals on the slope

lessons.title: Braking Fundamentals
lessons.introduction: Braking well means slowing down without losing traction or balance. The front brake does most of the stopping, the rear helps control speed, and your body position keeps the bike stable while you brake.
objectives: Stop smoothly using both brakes without skidding
Explain why the front brake provides most stopping power
Brake before a feature or corner, not in it

physics.summary: Braking shifts weight toward the front wheel. That extra load gives the front tyre more grip, which is why it can do more of the stopping, as long as your body is ready for it.

blocks.heading: Load moves forward when you slow down
blocks.body: When you brake, your body wants to keep moving forward. That pushes load onto the front tyre and takes it off the rear. More load on the front means more available grip there, and less at the back, so the rear wheel locks and skids more easily.

blocks.heading: Grip has a limit
blocks.body: A tyre can only provide so much friction. Squeezing the lever harder than the tyre can handle makes it skid, and a skidding tyre grips less than a rolling one. Smooth, progressive braking keeps you under that limit.

technique.title: One-finger braking
technique.result: Full control without losing your grip.
technique.movement: Use one finger on each lever, the rest wrapped round the grip. Set levers so your finger reaches them comfortably.
technique.interaction: Modern brakes are powerful enough that one finger is plenty.

technique.title: Brace for the stop
technique.result: Stay stable as load shifts forward.
technique.movement: Drop your heels and sink your hips back slightly as you brake, arms bent.
technique.interaction: Bracing through your feet stops you being pushed forward over the bars.
cues: Push the bike forward a little

technique.title: Brake before, release through
technique.result: Enter features at the right speed with tyres free to grip.
technique.movement: Do your braking on the straight before a corner or rough section, then ease off through it.
technique.interaction: Rolling tyres grip and track better than braking ones.

equipment: A bike in good working order, sized to fit you
protective: Flat or clip-in shoes with good grip
environments: Flat open area, then a gentle gravel or dirt slope
conditions: Avoid wet or loose surfaces while learning

lessons.title: Terrain Awareness Foundations
lessons.introduction: Terrain awareness is a skill of the eyes and brain. You learn to scan ahead, spot the important features, pick a line and then trust your body to ride what you've already seen.
objectives: Look further ahead than feels natural
Identify the main line through a section before riding it
Describe how speed changes how far ahead you need to look

physics.summary: Reaction time is roughly constant, so the faster you go, the further you travel before you can respond. Looking further ahead buys time.

blocks.heading: Speed turns time into distance
blocks.body: If it takes you about a second to notice and react to something, at 5 m/s you travel 5 m in that second; at 10 m/s, 10 m. Looking far enough ahead to see features well before you reach them is how you keep up as speed increases.

blocks.heading: Surfaces change your grip
blocks.body: Dry dirt, wet roots, loose gravel and rock all offer different amounts of friction. Spotting a change in surface early lets you brake, straighten up or change line before you're on it.

technique.title: Eyes up
technique.result: See features early enough to act.
technique.movement: Lift your gaze to look down the trail, then glance near only briefly.
technique.interaction: Your peripheral vision tracks what's close.
cues: Look to the next feature, then the one after

technique.title: Pick a line
technique.movement: Before a technical section, choose an entry, a path through and an exit.
technique.interaction: A clear plan reduces hesitation.
cues: Look where you want to go, not at what you want to avoid

equipment: A bike in good working order, sized to fit you
protective: Flat or clip-in shoes with good grip
environments: Easy trail with a mix of surfaces
conditions: Avoid wet or loose surfaces while learning

lessons.title: Direction Control Foundations
lessons.introduction: At slow speed you mostly steer with the bars. As speed rises, you increasingly turn by leaning the bike, and your eyes lead the way. This lesson covers both.
objectives: Steer a tight cone slalom at low speed
Lean the bike while keeping your body more upright
Explain why the bike leans when it turns

physics.summary: A turning bike needs a sideways force from the tyres toward the inside of the turn. Leaning lines up gravity and that sideways force so you stay balanced.

blocks.heading: Turning needs a sideways push
blocks.body: To follow a curved path, something has to push you toward the centre of the curve. On a bike that's friction between the tyres and the ground. Leaning the bike lets that sideways force and gravity combine through the tyres so you don't tip over.

blocks.heading: Counter-steering
blocks.body: At speed, a brief push on the bar on the inside of the turn starts the bike leaning that way. Most riders do this without noticing. At walking pace you steer the bars directly instead.

technique.title: Eyes lead
technique.movement: Turn your head and look through the turn before you start it.
technique.interaction: Your body and bike tend to follow your eyes.

technique.title: Lean the bike, not the body
technique.movement: Press the inside bar down to lean the bike while your body stays more upright.
technique.interaction: Keeps your weight over the tyre contact patches.
cues: Push the inside grip toward the ground

equipment: A bike in good working order, sized to fit you
protective: Flat or clip-in shoes with good grip
environments: Flat open area with cones, then easy trail
conditions: Avoid wet or loose surfaces while learning

lessons.title: Cornering Fundamentals
lessons.introduction: A good corner has three parts: get your speed right before it, lean the bike and look through it, and let it run out the exit. This lesson puts those together on flat turns and gentle berms.
objectives: Brake before the corner and release through it
Choose a wide entry, a late apex and a clean exit
Lean the bike while keeping weight on your outside foot

physics.summary: The faster you go and the tighter the turn, the more sideways grip you need. Berms help by turning some of that sideways force into a push into the ground.

blocks.heading: Speed and radius set the grip you need
blocks.body: The sideways force needed to turn grows with the square of your speed and shrinks as the turn gets wider. Double your speed and you need four times the grip. That's why braking before the turn and using a wider line both help.

blocks.heading: Why berms feel so good
blocks.body: On a banked turn, the ground is tilted toward the inside. Part of the force you need comes from the ground pushing straight up through your tyres, rather than relying only on sideways friction, so you can corner faster with the same grip.

technique.title: Set your speed
technique.result: Arrive at the right speed with brakes off.
technique.movement: Brake on the straight before the turn.
technique.interaction: Tyres need all their grip for turning.

technique.title: Wide in, tight middle, wide out
technique.result: A line that straightens the corner.
technique.movement: Enter wide, turn toward a late apex, then let the bike drift wide on exit.
technique.interaction: A straighter path means less grip needed.
cues: Look for the exit before the apex

technique.title: Outside foot down
technique.movement: On flat turns, drop your outside pedal and press through it while leaning the bike.
technique.interaction: Pushes the tyres into the ground.
cues: Bike leans, chest over the bars
errors: Inside pedal down hitting the ground

protective: Flat or clip-in shoes with good grip
environments: Wide, smooth flat corners, then berms on easy trail

lessons.title: Pressure Control Foundations
lessons.introduction: Pressing the bike into the ground (weighting) and letting it come up (unweighting) changes how hard your tyres press on the trail. Doing it at the right time adds grip, absorbs bumps and sets up lifts and jumps.
objectives: Absorb a small bump by letting the bike come up into your body
Push the bike into a dip to keep tyres in contact
Explain how weighting changes grip

physics.summary: When you push down on the bike, the ground pushes back harder, increasing the normal force and the grip available. When you lift your body, the force on the tyres briefly drops.

blocks.heading: Push down, get more grip
blocks.body: Friction depends on how hard the tyre presses into the ground. By driving your weight down through the pedals at the right moment, you increase that force briefly and gain grip. Rising up does the opposite, making the bike light.

blocks.heading: Absorbing is spreading force over time
blocks.body: Letting the bike come up into you over a bump spreads the impact over a longer time, so the peak force is smaller. Locked limbs mean a short, sharp hit.

technique.title: Absorb
technique.movement: As the front wheel meets a bump, let your arms bend so the bike rises toward you, then your legs as the rear wheel arrives.
technique.interaction: Your body stays at a steadier height.
cues: Let the bike come to you

technique.title: Extend
technique.movement: On the back side of a bump or into a dip, push the bike down and away.
technique.interaction: Tyres stay in contact and gain grip.

equipment: A bike in good working order, sized to fit you
protective: Flat or clip-in shoes with good grip
environments: Gentle rollers or a pump track, or a grassy slope with small bumps
conditions: Avoid wet or loose surfaces while learning

lessons.title: Pumping Foundations
lessons.introduction: Pumping means unweighting the bike as it rises up a roller and pushing it down the back side. Done in rhythm, you speed up without turning the pedals.
objectives: Carry speed round a pump track without pedalling
Time your push to the back side of each roller
Explain where the extra speed comes from

physics.summary: Pushing down on a downward slope adds energy. You do work with your legs and arms, and the slope converts that push into forward speed.

blocks.heading: Where the speed comes from
blocks.body: On the back side of a roller, the ground is tilted forward. When you push down into it, part of the ground's push-back points forward, adding speed. Lifting your body on the front side means less of your weight works against you on the way up.

blocks.heading: Rhythm matters
blocks.body: Pumping only adds speed if the push comes on the downslope. Pushing on the upslope slows you down. That's why timing, not strength, is the key.

technique.title: Light on the way up
technique.result: Avoid losing speed on the face.
technique.movement: As you reach a roller, let the bike come up into your body.
technique.interaction: Less force against the upslope.

technique.title: Push the back side
technique.movement: Drive the bike down the back side with arms and legs together.
technique.interaction: Converts your push into forward speed.
cues: Push the bike into the backside

equipment: A bike in good working order, sized to fit you
protective: Flat or clip-in shoes with good grip
environments: Pump track or rollers on a flow trail
conditions: Avoid wet or loose surfaces while learning

lessons.title: Front-Wheel Lift Foundations
lessons.introduction: A front-wheel lift comes from pushing down into the bike and then shifting your hips back, not from yanking on the bars.
objectives: Lift the front wheel a few centimetres on demand
Use a push-then-shift-back movement rather than pulling
Roll the front wheel onto a small step

physics.summary: Moving your hips back puts your centre of mass behind the rear axle, so your weight creates a torque that lifts the front wheel.

blocks.heading: The rear axle is the pivot
blocks.body: When the front lifts, the bike rotates around the rear tyre's contact point. If your centre of mass is in front of that point, gravity pulls the front down; move it behind and gravity helps hold the front up.

technique.title: Compress
technique.movement: From the ready position, push down into the bars and pedals.
technique.interaction: Stores energy in your body and the bike.

technique.title: Shift back
technique.movement: Push your hips back and straighten your arms. The front comes up.
technique.interaction: Centre of mass moves behind the pivot.

equipment: A bike in good working order, sized to fit you
protective: Flat or clip-in shoes with good grip
environments: Flat smooth area, then small curbs or roots

lessons.title: Bunny Hop Foundations
lessons.introduction: A proper bunny hop is two moves linked together: lift the front wheel, then lift the rear by driving the bars forward and letting your legs come up. Learn each part separately before linking them.
objectives: Lift the front wheel with a push and shift back
Lift the rear wheel by pushing the bars forward and bringing the feet up
Link both into a smooth hop over a low line

physics.summary: A hop uses timing to rotate the bike backward, then forward, while your body rises. Your legs provide the upward impulse.

blocks.heading: Two rotations
blocks.body: The front lift rotates the bike nose-up around the rear wheel. Pushing the bars forward then rotates it level again while you rise, lifting the rear. Timing the change between those rotations is the heart of the skill.

blocks.heading: Your body goes up first
blocks.body: Extending your legs moves your body upward. When the bike follows, it's because your hands and feet bring it up with you, not because you jump off it.

technique.title: Front lift
technique.movement: Compress, then shift your hips back to lift the front wheel.
technique.interaction: Bike rotates around the rear wheel.

technique.title: Push forward
technique.result: Level the bike and lift the rear.
technique.movement: As the front rises, extend your legs and push the bars forward and up.
technique.interaction: Bike rotates level while rising.
cues: Push the bars toward the sky in front

technique.title: Absorb the landing
technique.movement: Let your arms and legs bend as both wheels touch down.
technique.interaction: Spreads the landing force.

equipment: A bike in good working order, sized to fit you
environments: Flat smooth area with a soft line or low foam obstacle
conditions: Avoid wet or loose surfaces while learning
stop_conditions: You feel tired, frustrated or rushed
The surface becomes wet, muddy or loose

warnings: Clipless pedals can make a bunny hop feel easier but hide poor technique and make bail-outs harder. Learn on flat pedals.

lessons.title: Jumping Fundamentals
lessons.introduction: A good jump starts on the approach. Arrive at the right speed, stay centred, let the lip push the bike up into you, and then let it fly. Start on small tabletops where coming up short is safe.
objectives: Roll a tabletop and land on the deck at low speed
Absorb and extend through the lip to keep the bike level
Explain how speed and lip angle change your flight

physics.summary: Once you leave the lip, gravity is the only big force acting on you, so you follow a curved path (a parabola) set by your speed and the lip angle.

blocks.heading: Speed and lip angle decide where you land
blocks.body: At the lip, your velocity has a forward part and an upward part. Gravity slows the upward part and pulls you back down, but leaves the forward part alone. More speed or a steeper lip means more height and distance. That's why matching speed to the jump is the first skill.

blocks.heading: Why the bike pitches
blocks.body: If the rear wheel is pushed up harder than the front as it leaves the lip, the bike rotates nose-down in the air. Staying centred and letting the bike come up through the lip keeps it level. The simulation leaves this out: it treats you as a single point.

technique.title: Approach
technique.result: Arrive centred, at the right speed.
technique.movement: Ready position, brakes off before the lip, eyes on the landing.
technique.interaction: Predictable takeoff.

technique.title: Takeoff
technique.result: A level bike leaving the lip.
technique.movement: Let the bike come up into you on the face, then extend through the lip with legs and arms together.
technique.interaction: Even push from both wheels keeps the bike level.
cues: Let the lip come to you

technique.title: Flight and landing
technique.result: Calm in the air, soft on landing.
technique.movement: Stay relaxed, match the bike to the landing angle and absorb.
technique.interaction: Spreads the landing force.

equipment: A bike in good working order, sized to fit you
environments: Small, well-built tabletop jumps at a bike park or pump track
conditions: Avoid wet or loose surfaces while learning
stop_conditions: You feel tired, frustrated or rushed
The surface becomes wet, muddy or loose
Anything on the bike feels loose or wrong
warnings: Only ride jumps that are built for it, and inspect them first.
Never jump on unfamiliar features or jumps you can't see the landing of.

lessons.title: Landing Fundamentals
lessons.introduction: A good landing is about matching the bike's angle to the ground and spreading the impact through your arms and legs.
objectives: Land both wheels together or rear slightly first on a downslope
Absorb landings with bent limbs
Explain why downslope landings are softer than flat ones

physics.summary: Landing on a slope that matches your falling path turns the impact into forward speed. Landing to flat stops all your downward speed at once.

blocks.heading: Downslope landings are softer
blocks.body: If the landing slopes in the same direction you're falling, the ground only has to change your direction a little. On flat ground, all your downward speed has to stop at once, so the force is much bigger.

blocks.heading: Absorbing spreads the hit
blocks.body: The same change in momentum over a longer time means a smaller force. Bending your arms and legs on landing stretches out the time.

technique.title: Match the angle
technique.movement: In the air, adjust the bike to match the landing slope.
technique.interaction: Smoothest transition.
cues: Match the bike to the landing

technique.title: Absorb
technique.movement: Let your arms and legs bend as the wheels touch, then return to ready.
technique.interaction: Spreads the force over time.

equipment: A bike in good working order, sized to fit you
environments: Small rollers, then small drops with a downslope landing
conditions: Avoid wet or loose surfaces while learning
stop_conditions: You feel tired, frustrated or rushed
The surface becomes wet, muddy or loose
Anything on the bike feels loose or wrong

lessons.title: Manual Foundations
lessons.introduction: In a manual you balance on the rear wheel by holding your hips back over the rear axle. Your legs, hips and the rear brake keep you there. It's a balance skill, not a strength skill.
objectives: Find the balance point on the rear wheel
Use the rear brake to stop the bike from looping out
Hold a short manual on flat ground

physics.summary: A manual is balance on a single contact point. When your centre of mass is directly above the rear contact patch, there's no torque tipping you forward or back.

blocks.heading: The balance point
blocks.body: Too far forward and gravity brings the front down. Too far back and the bike loops out. The balance point is the narrow zone in between, where your centre of mass sits over the rear contact patch.

blocks.heading: The rear brake is your safety net
blocks.body: Dabbing the rear brake slows the rear wheel, which pitches the bike forward and brings the front down. That's how you recover when you go past the balance point.

technique.title: Brake covered
technique.result: A safety net before you start.
technique.movement: Keep a finger on the rear brake throughout.
technique.interaction: You can always bring the front down.
cues: Finger on the rear brake, always

technique.title: Push then hips back
technique.movement: Compress, then push your hips back and straighten your arms.
technique.interaction: Moves your centre of mass over the rear axle.

technique.title: Hold with your legs
technique.movement: Make small adjustments with your knees and hips; dab the rear brake if you go too far.
technique.interaction: Small movements change torque.
cues: Knees bend to drop the front, extend to raise it

equipment: A bike in good working order, sized to fit you
environments: Flat, smooth surface such as a car park or grass, away from traffic
conditions: Avoid wet or loose surfaces while learning
stop_conditions: You feel tired, frustrated or rushed
The surface becomes wet, muddy or loose
Anything on the bike feels loose or wrong
warnings: Looping out is a common fall. Always cover the rear brake, and learn on flat pedals so you can step off the back.

lessons.title: Drop Foundations
lessons.introduction: A small drop can be rolled. Larger drops need speed and a little front-wheel lift so the bike leaves the edge level and lands both wheels together.
objectives: Roll a small drop with good body position
Lift the front slightly off a drop to land level
Choose a speed that clears the edge to a downslope

physics.summary: Off a drop, your bike follows a curved path. Without enough speed or lift, the front wheel drops first because gravity acts on it as soon as it leaves the edge.

blocks.heading: Why the front drops first
blocks.body: When the front wheel leaves the edge but the rear is still on it, gravity pulls the front down while the rear is supported. The bike rotates nose-down. A small front lift or enough speed means the wheels leave closer together.

technique.title: Approach
technique.movement: Eyes on the landing, brakes off before the edge.
technique.interaction: A predictable departure.

technique.title: Lift and push
technique.result: A level bike in the air.
technique.movement: As the front reaches the edge, give a small front lift and push the bike forward.
technique.interaction: Counters the nose-down rotation.

equipment: A bike in good working order, sized to fit you
environments: Small, well-built drops with a clean downslope landing
conditions: Avoid wet or loose surfaces while learning

The surface becomes wet, muddy or loose
Anything on the bike feels loose or wrong

lessons.title: Bike Setup Fundamentals
lessons.introduction: You don't need to be a mechanic to set up your bike well. Tyre pressure, suspension sag and lever position are the three settings that make the biggest difference.
objectives: Set tyre pressure for your weight and terrain
Measure and set suspension sag
Position brake levers for one-finger braking

physics.summary: Lower tyre pressure gives a larger contact patch and more grip but less support. Suspension sag lets the wheels follow dips as well as bumps.

blocks.heading: Tyre pressure and grip
blocks.body: A tyre supports your weight with air pressure over its contact patch. Lower the pressure and the patch grows to support the same weight, giving more grip and comfort, but too low and the tyre squirms or the rim hits rocks.

blocks.heading: Why sag matters
blocks.body: Sag is how much the suspension compresses with you sitting or standing on the bike. That reserve lets the wheel extend into holes as well as compress over bumps, keeping the tyre on the ground.

technique.title: Tyre pressure
technique.movement: Start from the manufacturer's suggested range, then adjust a little at a time.
technique.interaction: Balances grip and protection.

technique.title: Set sag
technique.movement: Use the sag markers or an O-ring; adjust air until sag is in the manufacturer's range.
technique.interaction: Wheels can follow terrain.
cues: Follow your fork and shock's guide

technique.title: Lever position
technique.movement: Angle levers so your wrists are straight in the ready position and your finger reaches the lever end.
technique.interaction: Comfort and control.
cues: Straight wrists in the attack position

equipment: A bike in good working order, sized to fit you
protective: Flat or clip-in shoes with good grip
environments: At home or the trailhead, with a pump and shock pump
conditions: Avoid wet or loose surfaces while learning
stop_conditions: Any part feels loose after adjustment
Brakes feel spongy or weak
You're unsure a setting is within the manufacturer's range
warnings: Never exceed the pressure printed on the tyre or rim. Have a mechanic check anything you're unsure of.
